beats.narration_text: Run the same LLM on the same quote three times and you can get three different answers. I'm Anjana — here's the one number responsible: temperature.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'running the same prompt three times…'
output lines resolve: 'temperature zero locks the answer' / 'temperature one lets it drift' / 'self-consistency catches the difference'

props.segment: Temperature: The Dial Between Prediction and Hallucination
props.command: I ran the same earnings quote through an LLM three times and got three different extracted answers — same model, same prompt. Can you show me what's actually controlling that?
props.runningText: running the same prompt three times…

beats.narration_text: You give an LLM the same earnings call quote three times. Same model. Same prompt. But you get three different answers. The output changed because you turned one dial. Temperature.

show.event: three identical quote cards land in a row: 'We anticipate moderate revenue growth in the back half of the year.'
different extraction results fade in below each card — 'raised, 0.72' / 'maintained, 0.65' / 'raised, 0.81'; a question mark pulses above
'Temperature' lands large below the cards; a circular dial icon fades in beside it, needle at an ambiguous mid-point

beats.narration_text: Temperature controls randomness. At zero, the model picks the single most likely next token every time. Deterministic. Same input, same output, guaranteed. At zero point five, it considers a wider range of tokens. There is variation, but it stays close to the most probable answer. At one point zero, the distribution flattens. Rare tokens get a real chance. The model becomes creative. In fiction writing, that is interesting. In financial extraction, that is a hallucination.

show.event: T=0.0: one dominant bar towers over flat others in a token-probability chart; dial (top-left) points to 0.0; caption 'Deterministic. Same input → same output.'
dial animates to T=0.5: tallest bar shrinks ~30%, second/third bars grow; caption 'Slight variation. Mostly predictable.'
dial animates to T=1.0: distribution flattens dramatically, rare tokens get visible mass; caption 'Creative. Unpredictable.'; tallest bar's color shifts cool blue → warm red as the dial turns

beats.narration_text: Here is the same earnings quote run at three temperatures. At zero, the model says "maintained" with zero point seven one confidence. Run it again, same answer. And again, same answer. Locked. At zero point five, it says "maintained" twice, then "raised" once. Two out of three agree. At one point zero, it says "raised," then "maintained," then "lowered." Three runs, three different answers. None of them reliable. This is why financial extraction systems run at low temperature. And why self-consistency decoding runs the same prompt multiple times and votes. If the model cannot agree with itself, the answer is not stable enough to trust.

show.event: the earnings quote returns at top; three columns appear side by side, each headed by a temperature setting and dial position
column T=0.0: three identical rows ('maintained — 0.71' ×3, blue), lock icon, calm green border, label 'Stable.'
column T=0.5: three rows (two 'maintained' blue, one 'raised' green), amber border, '2/3 agree' tag, label 'Mostly stable.'
column T=1.0: three rows, three different directions/colors (raised/maintained/lowered), warning triangle, red border, label 'Unstable.'
a bracket draws around column T=0.5's three runs with an arrow to a verdict box: 'Vote → maintained (2/3)'; label 'Self-consistency: run multiple times, take the majority.'

props.sparkLine: If it can't agree with itself, don't trust it.

beats.narration_text: Temperature is one number. It controls whether your model gives you the same answer every time or a different answer every time. In finance, you want the first one. Creativity is for poets. Consistency is for predictions.

show.event: the dial returns, centered, large, set near zero — calm, steady
on 'Creativity is for poets' — the needle twitches toward 1.0, background flickers warm/chaotic, the T=1.0 flattened distribution briefly flashes
on 'Consistency is for predictions' — the dial snaps back to near-zero, background settles calm, the T=0.0 locked distribution reappears
title lands: 'Temperature.' / 'The dial between prediction and hallucination.'

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Temperature controls how the model samples its next token — at zero it's deterministic, always the top choice. Turn it up and the distribution flattens, letting rare tokens through. For financial extraction, that instability looks like a hallucination, not creativity. Which is why low temperature and self-consistency voting are the standard defense.

line 1: dial-at-zero icon settles in
line 2: flattening-distribution icon settles in
line 3: three-column comparison icon settles in
line 4: vote/checkmark icon locks in, largest element

props.artifactHeading: The dial between prediction and hallucination.
artifactLines: Temperature zero: greedy decoding, same input always gives the same output.
Higher temperature flattens the distribution — rare tokens get a real chance.
In finance, that flattening looks like a hallucination, not creativity.
Self-consistency runs the same prompt multiple times and takes the majority vote.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. "I use an LLM output for a task where I need the same input to give me the same answer every time, and I honestly don't know what temperature or sampling settings it's running at. Can you help me: one, figure out what temperature my current setup is actually using; two, tell me honestly whether that setting matches what the task needs — consistency or creativity; and three, if it's wrong, suggest a fix, including whether running the same prompt multiple times and voting would help?" Paste that into Claude and find out if your own pipeline has a temperature problem hiding in it.
